extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (Math 145) and other participants interested in undergraduate algebraic geometry (Stanford)
extracted.subtask_description: Syllabus and course policies for Math 145 (Undergraduate Algebraic Geometry): describes prerequisites, topics, expectations, grading, problem set rules, short writing assignment, and participation/contribution requirements for students and participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Comfort with rings and modules. At the very least, a strong background from Math 120. Background in commutative algebra, number theory, complex analysis (in particular Riemann surfaces), differential geometry, and algebraic topology will help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor aims to 'aim this class at people with a strong background in algebra and a willingness to develop geometric intuition, but to also have it accessible to those who have taken Math 120 and are willing to work hard and learn new things on the fly.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Course topics and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The syllabus will roughly cover: linear geometry (degree on); hypersurfaces; degree 2 (conics, pythagorean triples, quadrics); degree 3 (elliptic curves); algebraic sets (V and I; Zariski topology; Noetherian rings; irreducible components; Hilbert's Nullstellensatz; morphisms); affine algebraic varieties and morphisms; projective varieties; rational functions and rational maps; images of morphisms; elimination theory; fibers; calculus (derivatives and differentials), smoothness, dimension theory; algebraic curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllabus will evolve depending on the class; topics are presented in a rough order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading weights
rubrics_metrics.description: Final grade composition: 50% problem sets (including online check-ins), 30% participation (online participation includes editing of notes), 20% one topic written up (term paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The one-topic write-up is 'likely to be a page's worth, but in the notes or latexed.' Participation includes in-class and online activities (editing notes, piazza).

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem set schedule and submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem sets will come out on the weekend and be due in Laurent Cote's mailbox the next Friday at 4 pm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laurent 'may actually pick them up a little later, but makes no promises.' Specific due dates for each problem set are listed on the syllabus; there is also an online check-in component on Canvas accompanying many sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework late policy and drops
rubrics_metrics.description: One homework can be late, but with a 25 per cent penalty; late sets can be handed in up until the end of week 9 (Friday 4 pm in Laurent's mailbox). The lowest homework score will be dropped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful of the single-late allowance and the week 9 cutoff; plan collaboration and write-ups accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and attribution on problem sets
rubrics_metrics.description: You are encouraged to discuss the problems with each other (in person, or on piazza) but must credit people (and other sources) for ideas when writing up solutions, and you must write up solutions individually and independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit all collaborators and external sources; failure to attribute or to produce independent write-ups would violate course policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online check-in component
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an 'online check-in' component on Canvas associated with many problem sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online check-ins factor into the problem set/participation component; check Canvas for details and deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short writing assignment (term paper) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: You will write a short mathematical exposition for others in the class. The length should be at least a page, but not much longer. It will be due no earlier than the 9th week, but a draft is requested earlier. Topics should be set by about week 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Background sources may be any references (the syllabus suggests the listed references, google, and wikipedia). Sample topics are provided (Weierstrass P-function, rational points on elliptic curves, proof of Nullstellensatz, etc.). Some topics can be two-person projects ('2 people working together or sequentially?'). Many compositions become part of the Overleaf notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes editing and student contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be editing and reading the notes; for one of the classes you will be responsible for the notes and making them as useful and readable as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instructor states: 'You are not allowed to ever complain again about a mathematics text, until you make your day's notes a work of art.' Contributions to the notes may be incorporated into the shared Overleaf notes (many compositions now part of the Overleaf notes). Online participation includes editing of notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class participation and learning practices
rubrics_metrics.description: You should be active in class, keeping the instructor honest, and asking questions (no matter how silly you think they are). You should be testing your understanding by doing problems, discussing with friends, going to office hours, and discussing on Piazza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use office hours (instructor and course assistant times listed) and Piazza for discussion; active engagement is explicitly part of the grade (30% participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Access and enrollment note
rubrics_metrics.description: You needn't be a student in the class in order to participate; periodic email to participants will be sent through Canvas and interested people can be added to the mailing list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-enrolled participants can join the mailing list and follow the course; however, official policies (grading, submissions) presume enrolled students.
